papers.titleEn: Draw-Ratio-Programmed Liquid Crystal Elastomer Fibers for Controllable Unidirectional Contraction and Intelligent Textile Integration
papers.abstract: Liquid crystal elastomer (LCE) fibers are promising candidates for soft actuators. However, it remains difficult to combine a low-temperature actuation onset, room-temperature retention of a mechanically programmed length, and textile processability in a single LCE fiber. Inspired by the energy input, state retention, and triggered release sequence of biological latch-mediated spring actuation (LaMSA), this study combines continuous spinning with room-temperature post-curing draw-programming to fabricate a high-performance, unidirectionally contracting LCE fiber. UV curing establishes the permanent network and its reference length, whereas subsequent mechanical stretching writes a recoverable extended state without a second curing step. Wide-angle/small-angle X-ray scattering (WAXD/SAXS) measurements show increased axial orientation after programming, and tensile-mode DMA shows that the programmed state has a higher storage modulus E' and undergoes gradual softening between 30 and 54 °C under fixed-length test conditions. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) identifies a thermal transition over approximately 25-54 °C, with a peak at 42.5 °C. When the fiber is free to move, photothermal heating releases the programmed deformation and drives contraction toward the cured reference length. Endpoint photographs show retention of the programmed length for more than one month in the observed fiber, and a load-lifting demonstration reaches 1100 times the fiber weight. The λs = 3 fiber also exhibits a tensile strength of 5.6 MPa and an elongation at break of 174%, allowing continuous processing on an automated flat knitting machine. Local programming further enables artificial-muscle models, light-controlled mechanical switches that retain the actuated state, and cotton/LCE knitted structures. The resulting one-way program-retain-release response provides a material and device basis for soft systems in which the final recovered state is maintained without continuous holding power.
